types.name: Power / game-improvement
types.head: 105–115 in² (oversize)
types.for: Beginners and players with short, slow swings who need free power and a big sweet spot.

types.name: Tweener / modern all-round
types.head: 98–104 in²
types.for: Most club players: a blend of power, spin and control. The biggest category on the market.

types.name: Control / player's frame
types.head: 95–98 in²
types.for: Advanced players with long, fast swings who generate their own power and want feel and precision.

types.name: Junior
types.head: Varies by length
types.for: 19 in (under 5), 21 in (5–6), 23 in (6–8), 25 in (8–10), 26 in (10–11) then full size 27 in.

specs.what: String-bed area in square inches. Bigger = larger sweet spot and more power; smaller = more control and feel.
specs.range: 95 in² (control) to 115 in² (oversize). 98–100 is the sweet spot for most players.

specs.what: Heavier frames are more stable and plow through the ball; lighter frames are easier to swing but twist on off-centre hits.
specs.range: 250 g (light) to 340 g (pro). Most club players: 285–305 g.

specs.what: Where the weight sits. Head-light frames are manoeuvrable at net; head-heavy frames add power to short swings.
specs.range: Measured in points or cm from the butt. 32 cm = even balance for a 68.5 cm racket.

specs.what: How heavy the racket feels when you swing it. The single best predictor of stability and power.
How much the frame flexes. Stiff frames return more energy (power) but transmit more shock; flexible frames feel softer and more controlled.
specs.range: 55 RA (very flexible) to 72 RA (very stiff). Arm-friendly: under 65.

specs.what: Mains x crosses. Open patterns (16x19) grip the ball for spin; dense patterns (18x20) give control and string durability.
specs.range: 16x19 is the modern standard; 18x20 for flat hitters; 16x16 / 14x18 for spin.

specs.what: Thickness of the frame. Thicker = stiffer and more powerful.
Handle circumference. Hold the racket with an Eastern grip: your other hand's index finger should fit between fingertips and palm.
specs.range: L1 (4 1/8 in) to L5 (4 5/8 in). Most men L3, most women L2. When in doubt go smaller and add an overgrip.

specs.what: Standard is 27 in. Extended frames (27.5 in) add serve leverage but reduce manoeuvrability.

strings.feel: Softest, most powerful, holds tension best
strings.for: Arm problems, feel players, pros in hybrids
strings.examples: Babolat VS Touch, Wilson Natural Gut

strings.feel: Firm, low-powered, huge spin and control
strings.for: Hard hitters and string breakers; most pros
strings.cons: Loses tension fast, harsh on the arm, restring every 10–15 hours
strings.examples: Luxilon ALU Power, Babolat RPM Blast, Solinco Hyper-G
Prince Synthetic Gut, Gosen OG-Sheep Micro

strings.for: The pro standard: spin from the poly, comfort from the gut
strings.examples: Federer and Djokovic: gut mains / ALU Power Rough crosses

tension: Lower tension (20–23 kg / 45–50 lb) = more power, comfort and spin with poly. Higher tension (25–27 kg / 55–60 lb) = more control. Pros range from Nadal's ~25 kg to Sampras's ~34 kg of gut; modern poly users sit around 22–25 kg.

choose.advice: 100–105 in², 270–290 g, synthetic gut or multifilament at 23 kg. Prioritise a big sweet spot and comfort.
100 in² tweener, 290–300 g, 16x19, multi or soft poly. Demo three frames before buying.
98–100 in², 300–315 g, poly or hybrid. Choose by swingweight: 310–325 for stability.
Flexible frame (RA under 65), natural gut or multifilament, lower tension, larger grip. Avoid stiff frames with full poly.
